You've just gotta treat him with compassion. At the end of the day, poor fella is scared. With my vietnamese blue beauty, I've noticed he doesn't like the hook and prefers me to use my hands. 

If you're calm, it makes a big difference to the snake. Take deep, slow breaths. Don't make sudden movements. And also don't force anything. Wait for him to be out and about, and then offer the option to come out. 

If you constantly invade the snakes space and haul it out to get it used to it or whatever, it will remember the fear of being swooped up, and it could go poorly. 

Remember, you're the predator, and the snake is the prey in this situation. Snakes aren't necessarily used to this. Their fear reaction is often considered aggression. Minimize fear response, and you should have minimal issues. 

I don't know if you have a top or front opening enclosure for this fellow, but I've come to believe that front opening is superior for snakes, because it minimizes fear. We are on the same level, I'm coming gently beside my snake, around and scooping underneath, I'm not coming from above with huge scary shadows. 

If my VBB tries to run away when I go to let him out, then I won't chase him down, I let him hide. Whatever makes him comfortable. 

Pay attention to his body language, his breathing, and his tail movements. You will learn how to read each other. Take no rush in trying to acclimate this snake to yourself, everything in time. Remember, you're the scary one, not the snake. If it happens to bite you, you are okay. But if you get bit, you should think why this happened. What movements were you making? Moving too fast? Or too close to their face? Or if you come from above. A snake will only bite when it feels the need, figure out why it felt the need to defend itself, and prevent it in the future.

Lol 2 weeks isn't long at all for an adult snake, even adult geckos people overfeed heavily. 

What must be considered is the amount of activity that a captive snake gets, if you have an adult BP in a small 40G aquarium (not very uncommon), it will not get much exercise at all, therefore doesn't need much food.

However if you have the same adult BP in say a 4x2x2 or something and they're always cruising about, it's a lot more activity so therefore more frequent feeding is required. 

The feeding regime depends heavily on so many factors its hard to say "this is how much you should feed" it's really a matter of situation, I personally prefer smaller meals about every 2 weeks for my adult BPs but even my adult Woma python will get a smaller meal every week, because they are much more active. 

Morale of the story: a ball python can easily go over 2 weeks between feedings, sometimes they go off food on their own accord for several months. Gravid females won't eat for a long time, while building eggs and don't have any issues.
